THOUGHT: The patient is a 2-year-old immunocompetent child with multiple painless, nonpruritic, skin-colored, pearly papules featuring central umbilication—classical clinical morphology of molluscum contagiosum. The lesions are distributed on the abdomen and extremities, consistent with autoinoculation and contact transmission. The history of daycare attendance supports exposure to a common viral infection spread via direct skin-to-skin contact or fomites. The recent case in another daycare peer further strengthens the epidemiologic link. Although the brother had chickenpox (varicella-zoster virus) one month ago, varicella presents with pruritic, vesicular, crusting lesions in crops—not umbilicated papules—and would not explain this morphology. The absence of systemic symptoms, normal vital signs, and unremarkable CBC argue against bacterial infection, atypical mycobacterial disease, or systemic illness. Skin biopsy is not required for diagnosis in typical cases; the presence of Henderson-Paterson bodies would be confirmatory but is unnecessary here. Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a poxvirus (MCV), highly prevalent in young children, and self-limited—aligning perfectly with the clinical picture.

DIAGNOSIS: Molluscum contagiosum
